title: How a Database Stores Data: Pages, B-Trees, LSM Trees and the WAL
oneLiner: Pages and the buffer pool, the write-ahead log and crash recovery, B-trees versus LSM trees, and row versus column storage.
keyTakeaway: A commit is durable once its record is in the write-ahead log; data pages catch up later. B-trees update pages in place and read cheaply; LSM trees turn writes into sequential appends and pay with compaction and multi-file reads. Row stores suit transactions, column stores suit analytics.
explanation:
You can use a database for years without knowing how it stores data, until a design decision depends on it: which engine for a write-heavy workload, why random UUID keys slow inserts, how a crash mid-write doesn't corrupt anything. This lesson opens the box.

The LSM tree simulator lets you watch writes land in memory, flush to sorted files and get compacted, and see how many places a read has to check.
